messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 48
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Tutor
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 78

# Margaret

Margaret sits in the waiting room with her hands folded neatly in her lap, her posture rigid despite the comfortable chair. At forty-eight, she has the composed appearance of someone accustomed to presenting a careful version of herself to the world. She's a tutor—has been for nearly twenty years—and she carries that professional demeanor like armor.

The trauma began seven years ago, though Margaret doesn't mark time that way. She marks it by before and after. Before, she was someone who believed in second chances, who saw the best in people. Her husband, David, was charming in the early years of their marriage. But alcohol changed him. Or perhaps it revealed something that had always been there.

The night that fractured everything happened on a Tuesday. Margaret had corrected David about something trivial—she can't even remember what now—and he'd grabbed her by the throat and slammed her against the kitchen counter. The violence was sudden and complete. She remembers the shock more than the pain, the way her mind couldn't reconcile what was happening with the person standing in front of her. When he finally released her, she crumpled to the floor, gasping. He left the house. She sat there for three hours, unable to move, unable to call anyone.

She stayed for another four years after that. There were apologies, promises, counseling sessions he quit attending. There were long stretches of peace that made her believe things might change. But the violence returned in cycles—sometimes months apart, sometimes weeks. Each time, Margaret would tell herself it was her fault, that she'd provoked him, that she should have been more careful. She told no one. Her family in Southeast Asia knew nothing. Her colleagues at the tutoring center saw only the same competent, reserved woman who arrived on time and prepared her lessons meticulously.

Three years ago, after an incident that left her with a fractured wrist, Margaret finally left. The divorce was quiet, settled without drama. She moved into a small apartment and returned to her work. On the surface, everything appeared to resume. She tutors high school students in mathematics and English, preparing them for exams with the same precision she brings to everything. Her students like her. Parents request her specifically.

But Margaret has not returned to herself.

She startles at sudden movements. When a student drops a textbook, her heart races and her hands shake. She's hypervigilant in ways she doesn't fully acknowledge—always aware of exits, of who is behind her, of potential threats in ordinary spaces. Loud voices make her freeze. She's taken to wearing her hair down to cover the thin scar on her neck, though she knows most people wouldn't notice it.

Sleep is fragmented. She lies awake for hours, her mind cycling through the same memories, or she wakes gasping from nightmares she can't quite recall but that leave her drenched in sweat. Some nights she doesn't bother trying to sleep at all, instead grading papers or preparing lesson plans in the quiet hours before dawn.

She's withdrawn from her husband in every way except legally—they remain married because divorce felt like failure, and Margaret has always been someone who sees things through. But she flinches when he touches her. She's become someone she doesn't recognize, someone smaller and more frightened. She wonders sometimes if this is who she'll be forever: a woman going through the motions of her life while something essential remains trapped in that kitchen, gasping for breath.
